claims.text: Severe plastic deformation will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Severe plastic deformation will enhance the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
Performing severe plastic deformation within a sufficiently low temperature window limits atomic diffusion.
Phosphorus can retard the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases in the target alloys.
Keeping the deformation temperature sufficiently low prevents significant recrystallization.
The benefit of severe plastic deformation may diminish below a critical phosphorus concentration.
Severe plastic deformation induces a high density of defects, including stacking faults, twins, and disordered regions.
Defect-rich regions generated by severe deformation can develop into amorphous zones once a critical defect density is reached.
Phosphorus stabilizes deformation-generated defect-rich regions against crystallization.
A concentrated lattice-defect network raises the local free energy.
The deformation-generated defect network promotes the formation of amorphous regions.
Phosphorus impedes crystallization kinetics by slowing atomic diffusion.
Phosphorus impedes crystallization by disrupting atomic ordering tendencies.
Severe-plastic-deformation-treated samples will have a higher amorphous-phase fraction than conventionally processed samples.
Severe-plastic-deformation-treated samples will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than conventionally processed samples.
Severe-plastic-deformation-treated samples will resist crystallization during thermal annealing better than conventionally processed samples.
The intervention will work only in phosphorus-containing systems susceptible to defect-mediated amorphization.
Excessive or uncontrolled deformation may cause phase transformations unrelated to amorphous stabilization.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis predicts both improved glass-forming ability and enhanced thermal stability, whereas the predicted outcome uses 'and/or,' allowing success in only one outcome.

The hypothesis is conjunctive, but the falsification rule requires absence of improvement across all listed metrics; improvement in only one metric could avoid falsification even if the other promised benefit fails.
